items.title: Former Mississauga, Brampton MP Navdeep Bains wins Ontario Liberal leadership
items.summary: Former Brampton, Mississauga MP Navdeep Bains held on to maintain razor-thin 3rd-round win in weekend leadership race. Navdeep Bains won the Ontario Liberal leadership in the third round of voting on Nov. 21. The Ontario Liberal Party has announced former Brampton and Mississauga member of Parliament Navdeep Bains will be its next leader. Bains won the leadership in a party ballot by a slim margin on Nov. 21. 29 per cent of the vote. The leadership vote saw a 15 per cent increase in turnout from its last leadership vote, according to a press release by the Ontario Liberal Party. More than 20,500 Liberal party members cast votes, it stated. “I am honoured by the trust Ontario Liberals have placed in me,” Bains said in the press release. “Ontario’s moment is now — and Ontario Liberals are ready for it. ” Bains enters the provincial political arena after years split between federal politics, teaching and the private sector.

items.title: CCF to defend free expression in Mississauga election sign ban case
items.summary: BRAMPTON, ONT. – The Canadian Constitution Foundation (CCF) has been granted leave to intervene in an Ontario citizen’s challenge to the City of Mississauga’s total ban on election signs on public property. The case, Vezina v City of Mississauga, was brought by longtime political candidate Greg Vezina, whose campaign signs were removed from public property under the city’s strict by-law in 2019. Vezina unsuccessfully sought an injunction against the city to stop the enforcement of the by-law’s provisions during the October 2026 municipal election. Vezina’s application will now proceed to a hearing in the Superior Court of Justice to determine whether the by-law provisions in question amount to a limit on the freedom of expression protected by section 2(b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Vezina argues the sign by-law creates an unacceptable content-based restriction, meaning the city determines which signs are permitted based on the messages they convey. While the city prohibits election signs on public property, it permits other types of signs, including those advertising new housing developments and farmers’ markets. Mr. Vezina also argues the sign by-law creates a total ban on the type of expression in which he wishes to engage. Under section 1 of the Charter, total bans and content-based restrictions are difficult to justify. The CCF will assist the Court in identifying and analyzing content-based restrictions and total bans. Josh Dehaas, Interim Litigation Director for the CCF, said these kinds of sign bans put lesser-known candidates at a disadvantage when trying to reach voters. “Election signs are one of the few affordable ways new candidates can reach voters and compete with established politicians who already have name recognition,” said Dehaas. “Mississauga’s ban puts independent candidates and smaller parties at a serious disadvantage and imposes a restriction on political expression that the city must justify,” Dehaas added.

items.title: Correctional officer posed as cop at Toronto park, police say; Mississauga man charged
items.summary: A Mississauga man faces charges following an incident at a west-end Toronto park in which a correctional officer is alleged to have posed as a police officer while dealing with members of the public. m. this past Sunday in the parking lot at Colonel Sam Smith Park in the Kipling Avenue and Lake Shore Boulevard West area of Etobicoke. Police said a suspect who was employed at the time as a correctional officer at the Toronto South Detention Centre allegedly approached the occupants of a vehicle in the parking lot of the park and a verbal interaction ensued. The man reportedly identified himself as an Ontario Provincial Police officer and displayed a metal badge, Toronto Police said in a news release on Tuesday. He then “demanded identification from the occupants and directed them to exit their vehicle,” police added. A suspect was located nearby shortly after responding police officers arrived on the scene. items.title: Mississauga Arrest Closes In On Suspects Behind Welland Jewelry Store Break-In Attempt
items.summary: According to Niagara Regional Police, a Brampton man wanted in an attempted break-in at a jewelry store near Niagara Falls was arrested in Mississauga by Peel Regional Police on Monday. Police say he is now in custody awaiting a court appearance, and a second suspect is held by another police service pending transfer to Niagara police. Both men are suspects in an Oct. 26 attempted break-in at a jewelry store near Thorold Road and Prince Charles Drive in Welland, southwest of Niagara Falls. Police say a white Volkswagen Touareg SUV was used to ram the front of the business. The suspects could not get inside and fled in a black Audi Q7 at high speed before police arrived, Niagara police said in a news release. Detectives said two masked men were involved, and the building sustained significant damage, prompting a structural engineer to assess it.

items.title: If you’re looking for customer service, who are you going to call? 311!
items.summary: For the safest, fastest and most effective service, contact 311 through one of the City’s official channels. Whether they are reporting a pothole or maintenance concern, or asking about programs or property standards, residents can access hundreds of City services through a single point of contact: 311. 311 Mississauga is the City’s customer service hub, acting as the front door to non-emergency City information and service requests. Residents can ask questions, report concerns, get help navigating City services or be directed to appropriate outside sources. This direct connection helps the City respond to community needs and keep residents informed. ca, online, in person or through the City’s social media channels. Teletypewriter (TTY) service is also available at 905-896-5151 for people with hearing or speech-related disabilities. The centralized team connects residents with the right City service or department providing phone support in more than 240 languages and dialects, ensuring Mississauga’s diverse communities can access City services in a way that is inclusive, convenient and easy to understand. Contacting 311 directly means residents can be confident that their inquiry is entering the City’s official system, being directed to the appropriate area for action and can be tracked when follow-up is required. This direct connection helps improve accountability and helps residents receive accurate and consistent information. Often, 311 inquiries can be resolved quickly with the team providing information to a question, helping a resident use an online service or confirming the status of an existing request. In 2025, 73 per cent of calls were resolved at the first point of contact with no further action required. Resolving inquiries right away reduces unnecessary transfers and gives residents a faster, simpler and more streamlined experience.

items.title: Think twice before feeding wildlife in Mississauga
items.summary: It may seem kind, but it puts animals and people at risk. It’s also illegal, with a $365 fine for a first offence and higher penalties for repeat offences. A plate of chicken left in a park. Dog food dumped near a coyote den. Birdseed scattered in a parking lot. These may seem like small acts of kindness, but feeding wildlife does more harm than good. Mississauga is home to a variety of wild animals, including coyotes, foxes, squirrels, chipmunks and many species of birds. These animals are capable of finding food on their own and do not need our help. Giving a wild animal an easy meal may feel compassionate, but it can put the animal at risk. The best way to help is simple: do not feed wildlife. Wild animals normally keep their distance from people. When they are regularly fed, they can lose that natural fear and their behaviour can become unpredictable. They may linger in busy areas or get too close to people while looking for food. For example, a coyote that learns to associate people with food may begin approaching people instead of keeping its distance.

items.title: Second Officer Tells Francique Inquest Surveillance, Not a Planned Arrest, Was Underway That Night
items.summary: According to testimony at the coroner's inquest into the death of Jamal Francique, Det. Mani Sharifi said police had no plan to arrest Francique on the night he was fatally shot in 2020. Sharifi told the inquest officers moved in only after they observed Francique breaching his bail conditions by leaving his home. The real plan, Sharifi said, was to continue surveillance that had already been underway for roughly three or four days until an opportunity arose. A juror asked why Francique was not arrested earlier in the week, once officers first saw him breach his bail, and Sharifi said his unit was instead focused on investigating whether Francique possessed a firearm or was involved in drug activity. Francique was shot by an officer outside a Mississauga townhouse complex on the evening of Jan. 7, 2020, according to the inquest.

items.title: Dixie Road Shut Down in Both Directions After Crash Involving a Police Cruiser
items.summary: According to Peel Regional Paramedic Services, one person was taken to hospital with minor, non-life threatening injuries after a two-vehicle collision involving a police cruiser in Mississauga on Monday night. Paramedics say the crash happened on Dixie Road north of Rathburn Road. The other driver involved remained at the scene, paramedics said. Dixie Road is currently closed in both directions between Rathburn Road and Burnhamthorpe Road while crews respond, according to police. Police are asking motorists to seek alternate routes while the road remains closed.

items.title: Rooftop Solar and Two EVs Help Mississauga Couple Cut Energy Bills Well Below National Average
items.summary: According to CityNews Toronto, Mississauga residents Harminder Dhillon and Jyoti Grewal say they spent roughly $1,100 in 2025 to power their home and run two electric vehicles. The couple installed rooftop solar panels, disconnected natural gas service, switched to heat pumps and an induction stove, and replaced gas powered cars with electric ones, bringing their reported costs to about $92 a month. Canadian households spent an average of $4,943 on energy in 2023, according to Natural Resources Canada's Energy Fact Book. The outlet notes the figures come from different years and are not a direct comparison, since energy costs vary with home size and local rates. Dhillon, an engineer turned criminal lawyer, says the switch began as a response to climate change rather than an effort to save money, describing it to CityNews as a climate decision, not a financial one.
